questions.stem: A cancer screening program reports that people whose tumors were found by screening survive an average of two years longer after diagnosis than people diagnosed after symptoms appeared, yet the average age at death is unchanged between the two groups. Which explanation fits this pattern best?

options.text: Length-time bias, because slower-growing tumors are preferentially detected during screening rounds
Lead-time bias, because earlier detection lengthens the measured survival interval without postponing death
Selection bias, because healthier and more health-conscious volunteers chose to enroll in the program
Overdiagnosis, because the program detected tumors that would never have produced any symptoms

rationales.whyCorrect: Lead time is the interval by which screening advances the date of diagnosis. When the age at death is identical between groups, the extra 'survival' is purely an artifact of starting the clock sooner, which is the signature of lead-time bias. The other options name genuine screening biases and harms, but each would be expected to shift the distribution of tumor types or of deaths, not merely stretch the diagnosis-to-death interval while leaving age at death untouched.
rationales.eli10: Think of two runners who cross the finish line at the exact same second, but one of them started her stopwatch two miles earlier. Her recorded 'time on the course' looks much longer, even though she did not finish one moment later. Screening starts the stopwatch earlier by finding disease before symptoms, so 'years survived after diagnosis' stretches out even when the person dies on the very same day they would have anyway. That artificial stretch has a name: lead time.

questions.stem: Applying classic screening criteria (Wilson and Jungner), which condition is the strongest candidate for a population screening program?

options.text: A condition with a recognizable latent or early symptomatic stage for which an effective, accepted treatment exists
A rare condition that is uniformly fatal and for which no effective treatment is currently available anywhere
A condition whose natural history is poorly understood but that generates a high level of public concern
A condition detectable only by an expensive procedure that is unavailable outside specialty referral centers

rationales.whyCorrect: The Wilson and Jungner framework, still the reference point for WHO and national screening bodies, requires an important health problem with a detectable preclinical phase, an adequately understood natural history, an acceptable and accurate test, available diagnostic and treatment facilities, and, critically, an accepted treatment that works better when started early. Without an effective early intervention, screening only advances the date of bad news while adding cost and harm. Options B, C, and D each fail one or more of these prerequisites.
rationales.eli10: Screening pays off only when two things are true at the same time: the problem is already present but silent, and you can actually do something about it during that silent window. It is like checking your car's oil — low oil gives no warning sound, and topping it up genuinely prevents engine damage. Looking for something you cannot detect before symptoms, or cannot change even after you find it, just delivers the worry sooner without changing what happens.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates selective (targeted) screening rather than universal (mass) screening?

options.text: Offering blood pressure measurement to every adult who walks through a community health fair
Testing every newborn in the state for a standard panel of metabolic and genetic conditions
Offering low-dose CT lung cancer screening only to adults ages 50 to 80 with a 20 pack-year smoking history
Providing vision and hearing checks for all children entering kindergarten in a school district

rationales.whyCorrect: Selective or targeted screening restricts an offering to a subgroup defined by elevated risk, whereas mass screening is offered to an entire population or age cohort regardless of individual risk. Current USPSTF guidance limits low-dose CT to adults ages 50 to 80 with at least a 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years, precisely because radiation exposure, false positives, and invasive follow-up make the benefit-harm balance favorable only where baseline risk is high. Options A, B, and D are applied to everyone in a defined population group.
rationales.eli10: Universal screening is handing an umbrella to everyone in the city. Targeted screening is handing them out only on the side of the street where it is actually raining. CT scans deliver radiation and can set off a chain of follow-up scans and lung biopsies, so we aim them at the group whose chance of having cancer is high enough that what we catch outweighs what we cause. Same test either way — who gets offered it is the entire point.

questions.stem: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force assigns a screening service a grade of D. What does that grade signify for practice?

options.text: Evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms, so clinicians should convey that uncertainty
There is at least moderate certainty that the net benefit is small, so the service is offered selectively
There is moderate or high certainty of no net benefit, or that harms outweigh benefits, so use is discouraged
There is at least moderate certainty of a moderate to substantial net benefit, so the service is offered routinely

rationales.whyCorrect: USPSTF grade D is an active recommendation against a service, based on moderate-to-high certainty that it produces no net benefit or that harms outweigh benefits; the stated suggestion for practice is to discourage its use, which is what option C says. Option A describes an I statement, B describes grade C (offer selectively based on professional judgment and patient preferences), and D describes grades A and B. The distinction matters because grade D reflects demonstrated screening harms such as unnecessary biopsies, overtreatment, and false reassurance, not merely an absence of evidence.
rationales.eli10: Treat the grades as four different pieces of advice, not a report card where D just means 'bad grade.' A and B mean the evidence says do this. C means it depends on the individual person. D means the evidence says this does more harm than good, so steer away. And an I statement means we genuinely do not know yet. The trap is reading D as 'unproven' — it is not; D means someone looked and found the harms winning.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates overdiagnosis resulting from a screening program?

options.text: A screening test fails to flag an aggressive tumor, which becomes symptomatic several months afterward
A screening result is reported as positive, but the confirmatory biopsy shows no malignancy is present
Screening detects a small, indolent tumor that would never have produced symptoms during the person's lifetime
Screening detects disease at an early stage, but the person declines the treatment that is subsequently offered

rationales.whyCorrect: Overdiagnosis is the detection of real disease, confirmed on pathology, that would never have caused symptoms or death had it gone undetected. It differs fundamentally from a false positive (option B), where no disease exists, and from a false negative (option A). Overdiagnosis matters because it reliably leads to overtreatment, converting a healthy person into a patient who absorbs the risks of surgery, radiation, or medication with no possible benefit, and it cannot be identified in any individual patient at the time of diagnosis.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a home inspection turning up a hairline crack in the foundation. The crack is genuinely there, so this is not a false alarm. But it was never going to widen enough to matter for the life of that house. Once it is written into the report, though, the owner pays to have the foundation redone, with all the mess and expense that involves. Screening does the same thing with real but harmless disease: a true finding whose only real consequence is the treatment it sets in motion.

questions.stem: Screening programs are best evaluated by comparing disease-specific mortality between randomized screened and unscreened groups rather than by comparing survival time among people whose disease was detected. What is the primary reason for this preference?

options.text: Survival must be tracked through individual follow-up, whereas mortality can be drawn from existing vital records
Survival comparisons are inflated by lead time, length bias, and overdiagnosis, whereas mortality rates are not
Survival is calculated only among people who complete every screening round, so those who drop out are omitted
Survival estimates require complete tumor staging data, which population registries frequently record incompletely

rationales.whyCorrect: Survival measured from the date of diagnosis is distorted by three screening-specific artifacts: lead time advances the diagnosis date, length bias preferentially detects slow-growing disease with inherently better prognosis, and overdiagnosis adds cases that were never destined to be fatal. Disease-specific mortality in a randomized comparison counts deaths per population over a fixed period and is immune to all three. The other options name real practical inconveniences of survival data, but none of them is the reason survival is considered structurally misleading for judging screening.
rationales.eli10: If you judge screening by 'how long people live after we find it,' you are measuring with a ruler that screening itself bends. It starts the clock early, it disproportionately catches the slow gentle cases, and it counts findings that were never dangerous as successes. So instead, count how many people in a large group actually die of the disease over the same stretch of years. Nobody's date of death shifts merely because of when someone looked, so that number cannot be fooled by any of the three tricks.

questions.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes law, professional standards, and organizational policy as they shape screening in the United States?

options.text: USPSTF grades are federal regulations that clinicians are legally required to follow, while newborn screening panels are optional hospital protocols
USPSTF grades are expert evidence appraisals that federal law ties to no-cost-sharing coverage, while newborn screening panels are set by state law
Newborn screening panels are voluntary guidelines adopted hospital by hospital, while USPSTF grades create legally binding statewide screening mandates
Preventive coverage rules are written by professional nursing organizations, while USPSTF grades operate only as internal organizational policy

Braidwood Management (June 2025), so the requirement remains in force. Newborn bloodspot screening, by contrast, is mandated by individual state statutes, which is why panels vary from state to state even though a federal Recommended Uniform Screening Panel exists as advisory guidance.

First, a panel of experts reads the studies and says what actually works — that is a recommendation, and it persuades rather than compels. Second, Congress passed a law saying insurers must cover the top-rated ones without charging you at the counter — that is a coverage requirement. Third, your state legislature passed its own law requiring every newborn's heel to be pricked before discharge. Knowing which layer you are standing on tells you what is strongly advised versus what is legally required.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines a communicable disease?

options.text: An illness caused by an infectious agent that can be transmitted from a reservoir to a susceptible host
An illness caused by an infectious agent that produces disease only in people whose immune defenses are already weakened
An illness caused by tissue damage from a chemical, radiologic, or physical agent in the environment
An illness that appears in an unusually large number of people in a community within a short period of time

rationales.whyCorrect: A communicable (infectious) disease is defined by transmissibility: a pathogen leaves a reservoir and reaches a susceptible host by direct or indirect means. Transmissibility, not severity, host immune status, or case count, is the defining feature. Option D describes an outbreak or epidemic, option B describes opportunistic infection (a subset of infections, and not all opportunistic agents are communicable), and option C describes a noninfectious environmental illness. The definition matters because it points directly to the control strategies used in public health, each of which targets one link in the chain of infection.
rationales.eli10: Think about a cold going around your class versus a broken arm. A broken arm cannot jump to your friend; a cold can. 'Communicable' shares a root with 'communicate' - the germ gets passed along like a message. So the test is not how bad the illness is, how many people have it, or who is vulnerable to it. The only question is whether the agent can travel from its reservoir - a person, an animal, or a place like water or soil - into a new host.

Transmissibility, not severity, host immune status, or case count, is the defining feature. questions.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes quarantine from isolation?

options.text: Quarantine applies to people with laboratory-confirmed infection, and isolation applies to people who are still awaiting test results
Quarantine restricts the movement of people who were exposed but are not known to be sick; isolation separates people known to be infected
Quarantine may be ordered only by federal authorities, while isolation may be ordered only by state and local health authorities
Quarantine is used for diseases spread through the air, while isolation is used for diseases spread by contact or by droplets

options.text: Reservoir
Portal of entry
Susceptible host
Mode of transmission

The reservoir is the house, the mode of transmission is the trip, and the portal of entry is the front door of the next house.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if two-dose MMR coverage in a community fell from roughly 95% to roughly 80%?

questions.stem: Which comparison of the incubation period and the period of communicability is accurate?

options.text: The two describe the same interval, viewed from the perspective of the host in one case and of the pathogen in the other
Incubation runs from exposure until full recovery, and communicability begins only after all symptoms have completely resolved
Incubation runs from exposure to symptom onset, communicability is the interval when the agent can be transmitted, and the two can overlap
Incubation always ends before communicability begins, which is why screening people for symptoms is sufficient to halt spread

rationales.whyCorrect: Incubation describes the host's clinical timeline from exposure to first symptoms, while communicability describes the window during which the agent is shed and can reach a new host. These are separate intervals measured on different scales, and for many pathogens they overlap, meaning a person can be infectious before feeling ill; measles, for example, is contagious from four days before the rash appears. That overlap is why symptom-based control alone is incomplete and why exposure-based measures such as contact tracing and quarantine are added.
rationales.eli10: Incubation is the quiet stretch: the agent has moved in and is multiplying, but you feel nothing yet, like dough rising before it looks like bread. Communicability is whenever the agent is actually being shed into the world. Those are two separate stopwatches, and nothing forces them to start or stop together. When they overlap, someone can say 'I feel completely fine' and be telling the truth while still handing the agent to the next person.

These are separate intervals measured on different scales, and for many pathogens they overlap, meaning a person can be infectious before feeling ill; measles, for example, is contagious from four days before the rash appears. questions.stem: Which example best illustrates vector-borne transmission?

options.text: A child develops hepatitis A after eating fresh produce that was rinsed in contaminated water
A person develops West Nile virus infection after being bitten by an infected mosquito
A resident inhales droplet nuclei containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis in a poorly ventilated room
A newborn acquires group B streptococcal infection while passing through the birth canal

questions.stem: What is the primary public health purpose of contact tracing during a communicable disease investigation?

options.text: To estimate how many people in the surrounding population currently have the disease at a given point in time
To confirm that the laboratory method used to diagnose the index case produced an accurate result
To identify exposed people so they can be notified, monitored, and offered testing, prophylaxis, or quarantine before they transmit
To determine which person introduced the disease into the community so that legal penalties can be applied to that individual

rationales.whyCorrect: Contact tracing is a forward-looking control measure: it converts knowledge of one case into protective action for the people that case may have exposed. Interventions offered to contacts, including testing, post-exposure prophylaxis, vaccination, and quarantine, interrupt onward transmission during the window before contacts become infectious themselves. It is a confidential public health service, not a punitive process; contacts are notified of their exposure without revealing the index patient's identity, and that confidentiality is what sustains the cooperation the method depends on.

Contact tracing reaches the dominoes standing next to it and taps them: you were near someone infectious, here is a test, a preventive medication, or a plan for the next several days. The timing is the whole point - reach people during the quiet stretch, before they can pass anything on. And the index patient's name is never disclosed, because tracing only works if people are willing to name their contacts.

questions.stem: A public health department treats active tuberculosis using directly observed therapy (DOT), in which a trained worker watches the patient swallow each dose. What is the primary reason this approach is used?

options.text: It permits airborne precautions to be discontinued on the first day that antituberculosis treatment is started
It shortens the standard treatment regimen, so that substantially fewer total doses of medication are required
It replaces the need for a contact investigation, because patients under observation are no longer able to infect others
It supports completion of the full multidrug regimen, curing the patient and limiting emergence of drug-resistant tuberculosis

DOT does not shorten the regimen, does not replace contact investigation, and does not change the criteria for discontinuing infection-control precautions.

questions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes how notifiable disease reporting works in the United States?

options.text: One federal statute lists the reportable conditions, so clinicians in every state must report the same diseases to CDC
Each hospital sets its own reporting policy, so requirements differ by facility rather than by state or territory
Clinicians report cases directly to the World Health Organization, which then notifies state and federal health agencies
State and territorial laws set which conditions are reportable, and jurisdictions then share those data with CDC voluntarily

questions.stem: Measles virus can remain suspended in the air and infectious for up to two hours after an infected person has left a room. Which precaution category matches this transmission route?

options.text: Airborne precautions, added to standard precautions for agents carried on small particles that travel over distance
Contact precautions, because the agent spreads mainly by way of contaminated surfaces and unwashed hands
Droplet precautions, used for agents carried in large respiratory particles that settle within a few feet of the source
Standard precautions alone, since these are applied to every patient regardless of the suspected diagnosis

Standard precautions apply to every patient but are not sufficient alone, which is why transmission-based precautions are layered on top.

You need a respirator that seals to your face and room air that is actively pulled out and filtered. Floating means airborne.

questions.stem: Which comparison of disease elimination and disease eradication is accurate?

options.text: Elimination means worldwide case counts have fallen below one thousand per year, while eradication means they have fallen below one hundred per year
Elimination refers to preventing all deaths from a disease, while eradication refers to preventing all new infections within one defined region
Elimination applies only to vaccine-preventable diseases, while eradication applies to any disease for which effective curative treatment exists
Elimination is interruption of sustained local transmission in a defined area, so imported cases can still cause outbreaks; eradication is worldwide reduction to zero

rationales.whyCorrect: Elimination is geographically bounded and reversible: it means continuous (endemic) transmission has been absent from a defined area for at least 12 months, though importation can reseed outbreaks whenever population immunity slips. Eradication is ants no longer existing anywhere on Earth - you throw the traps away and never think about it again. Smallpox is the only human disease we have ever done that to. Measles shows the difference painfully: the Americas held elimination for years and then lost it once coverage slipped and transmission restarted.

options.text: Give MMR vaccine and immune globulin at the same visit, so the infant receives both immediate and long-lasting protection
Give MMR vaccine today, because vaccine given within 72 hours of exposure can prevent or modify measles in exposed contacts

Provide no prophylaxis, and advise the family to watch for fever and rash and to call the clinic if those symptoms appear

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the focus of environmental health as a field within public health?

options.text: The study of inherited genetic traits that determine an individual's susceptibility to chronic disease
The measurement of personal health behaviors such as diet, physical activity, tobacco use, and sleep patterns
The delivery of clinical treatment and rehabilitation services to people already living with a diagnosed illness
The assessment and control of physical, chemical, and biological conditions outside the body that affect health

The distractors name genetics, clinical care, and personal behavior, all of which influence health but none of which capture the external-exposure focus that defines the field.
rationales.eli10: Health problems come from different addresses. Some live in your DNA, some in your daily habits, and some in the air, water, soil, and buildings around you. Environmental health works on that third address. Since an exposure reaches everyone who lives in the same place, the fix is usually to change the place, by filtering the water or removing the hazard, rather than changing one person at a time.

questions.stem: In the United States, what is the most common source of lead exposure for young children?

options.text: Lead solder and lead service lines that release lead into a building's tap water
Imported spices, candies, and traditional remedies that have been contaminated with lead
Lead-contaminated house dust and soil produced by deteriorating paint in pre-1978 housing
Take-home dust carried on the clothing of a parent whose job involves working with lead

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC identifies lead dust as the most common source of lead exposure in young children, and the dominant reservoir generating that dust is residential lead-based paint, banned for residential use in 1978. As the paint chalks, abrades at friction surfaces such as windows and doors, or is disturbed during renovation, it produces fine particles that settle on floors and sills and contaminate adjacent soil, which children ingest through ordinary hand-to-mouth behavior. Lead service lines and solder, imported spices and remedies, and take-home occupational dust are all documented pathways but account for far fewer exposures. CDC's blood lead reference value of 3.5 mcg/dL flags children whose levels exceed roughly 97.5 percent of US children ages 1 to 5; it is a screening trigger rather than a safety threshold, since no blood lead level is considered safe, so eliminating the source is the intervention.
rationales.eli10: Lead paint does not have to be eaten in chips to cause harm. Every time a painted window slides or a door rubs its frame, a little of that old paint grinds into powder too fine to see. It settles on floors and sills and washes out into the yard. A toddler's hands live on those surfaces, and toddlers' hands go to their mouths dozens of times an hour. That steady, invisible dust, not one dramatic event, is where most childhood lead comes from.

questions.stem: Which statement about radon is accurate?

options.text: It is a colorless, odorless radioactive gas that seeps into buildings from the surrounding soil and rock
It is a colorless gas produced by incomplete combustion in furnaces, stoves, and unvented space heaters
It is a bacterial contaminant of private well water that causes acute gastrointestinal illness
It is a fibrous mineral once used in building insulation that causes mesothelioma decades later

rationales.whyCorrect: Radon is a colorless, odorless, tasteless radioactive gas formed by the decay of uranium in soil and rock; it enters buildings through foundation cracks, sump openings, crawl spaces, and gaps around utility penetrations and then accumulates indoors. EPA recommends mitigation at or above an action level of 4 pCi/L, suggests considering it between 2 and 4 pCi/L, and notes that no exposure level is risk-free. EPA estimates radon causes about 21,000 US lung cancer deaths per year, making it the second leading cause of lung cancer overall after smoking and the leading cause among people who have never smoked. Because the senses cannot detect it, testing is the only way to know a building's level, and mitigation typically uses sub-slab depressurization plus sealing. Option B describes carbon monoxide and option D describes asbestos, two indoor hazards frequently confused with radon.
rationales.eli10: Uranium is scattered through ordinary rock and soil, and as it breaks down it releases a gas. That gas drifts up through cracks in a foundation, and a heated building behaves like a chimney that gently pulls it in and holds it. Nothing about it registers: no smell, no color, no irritation. questions.stem: An occupational health team wants to reduce workers' exposure to a hazardous cleaning solvent. According to the hierarchy of controls, which approach is expected to be most effective?

options.text: Requiring each worker to wear a fit-tested respirator and chemical-resistant gloves for the task
Rotating staff so that no employee spends more than two hours per shift in the solvent area
Installing local exhaust ventilation that captures solvent vapors at the workstation
Switching to a less toxic water-based product that performs the same cleaning job

rationales.whyCorrect: NIOSH ranks control strategies from most to least effective as elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment. No option here offers elimination, so substitution is the highest level available: replacing the agent removes the hazard itself, so protection no longer depends on a fan running, a schedule being honored, or a respirator being worn and sealed correctly. Option C is an engineering control and the next best choice, option B is administrative, and option A is PPE, which ranks last because it protects one worker at a time and fails silently when it is misused, degraded, or omitted. The same reasoning drives community environmental practice, where replacing lead service lines outranks distributing point-of-use filters.
rationales.eli10: Rank the options by how much each one depends on a person doing the right thing every single time. A respirator protects only if it is worn, fitted, and maintained, so one rushed day erases it. A rotation schedule works only if it is followed. Ventilation works unless the fan fails. Swapping the chemical for a safer one keeps working when everyone is tired, new, or short-staffed. The fewer human decisions a control needs, the higher it sits.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains why young children generally receive a higher dose of environmental contaminants than adults living in the same setting?

options.text: They take in more air, food, and water per pound of body weight and often mouth hands and objects
They have a higher percentage of body fat, so more of each contaminant is stored than excreted
Their skin and airway linings are thicker and less permeable, which keeps contaminants circulating
Their resting metabolic rate is slower, so contaminants are broken down and cleared more gradually

rationales.whyCorrect: Pound for pound, children inhale more air and consume more food and water than adults, so an identical ambient concentration delivers a higher dose per kilogram of body weight. Behavior compounds this: crawling and playing on floors, carpets, and soil, combined with frequent hand-to-mouth activity, greatly increases ingestion of contaminated dust. Children also absorb a substantially larger fraction of ingested lead from the gut than adults, and their developing neurologic, endocrine, and respiratory systems are more vulnerable to injury, with a longer remaining lifespan for latent effects to emerge, which is why children are often used as the sentinel population when standards are set. The distractors invert real physiology: after infancy young children have proportionally less body fat than adults, thinner and more permeable skin and airway linings, and a higher rather than lower resting metabolic rate.
rationales.eli10: Dose is not how much is in the air, it is how much lands in a body of a given size. A toddler moves a lot of air and water through a very small body, so the same room delivers a bigger hit per pound, the way a tablespoon of salt tastes very different in a cup than in a stockpot. Then add where they spend the day, down on the floor where dust settles, with hands going in and out of their mouths.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates the concept of environmental justice?

options.text: A city mails free radon test kits to every household on identical terms in all neighborhoods
A low-income area carrying a disproportionate pollution burden gains real influence over permitting
A state raises residential trash collection fees by the same percentage in every county
A manufacturer voluntarily posts its annual air emissions figures on its corporate website

rationales.whyCorrect: Environmental justice, as the term is used in public health, has two linked components: fair treatment, meaning no population group bears a disproportionate share of environmental burdens, and meaningful involvement, meaning affected residents have genuine influence over decisions affecting their environment. Option B is the only choice addressing both the distributive question of cumulative burden and the procedural question of community voice. The other options describe defensible environmental health practices, but uniform test-kit distribution and a uniform fee increase deliver identical treatment, which is equality rather than equity, and voluntary disclosure supplies information without altering who is exposed or who decides. Note also that environmental justice is a guiding equity principle whose enforceable weight varies by jurisdiction, since some states have enacted cumulative-impact permitting statutes while others have not.
rationales.eli10: Two ideas hide inside the term, and you need both. The first is about the load: if every landfill, highway, and smokestack ends up in the same few square miles, that is not a fair share, however legal each individual permit was. The second is about the microphone: the people who breathe the air are in the room when the next permit is decided, not merely notified afterward. Treating every neighborhood identically does nothing about a load that was never distributed evenly to begin with.

questions.stem: Which change to a community's built environment would most likely increase residents' routine daily physical activity?

options.text: Building connected sidewalks, protected bike lanes, and safe crossings to shops and transit
Distributing free pedometers and printed exercise guides at the neighborhood community center
Offering discounted memberships at a fitness center located twelve miles from the neighborhood
Posting motivational signs in office lobbies that urge employees to choose stairs over elevators

rationales.whyCorrect: The built environment, meaning human-made surroundings such as street layout, land use, sidewalks, transit, and parks, determines how much incidental activity occurs without anyone deciding to exercise. Street connectivity, mixed land use, and safe crossings make walking and cycling the convenient default for errands, school, and commuting, so the benefit reaches the entire population passively and persists as long as the infrastructure does. The remaining options are individual-level informational or access strategies that require sustained motivation, reach mainly those already interested, and decay once the campaign ends; option C additionally places the resource beyond walking or transit range of the residents it is meant to serve. This is why environmental modification generally produces broader and more durable population effects than information alone.
rationales.eli10: Ask what the neighborhood makes easy. If the only route to the grocery store is a highway shoulder with no sidewalk, a pedometer just measures how little you walked. Build a connected route with safe crossings and walking becomes the ordinary way to get milk, with no decision, no willpower, and no sign-up. Information asks people to overcome their surroundings; design changes what the surroundings ask of them.

questions.stem: A community's Air Quality Index for fine particulate matter is reported as 165, which falls in the red 'Unhealthy' category. What does this reading indicate for the community?

options.text: Only residents with previously diagnosed asthma are affected; other residents face no added risk
Outdoor exercise is safe for everyone provided residents keep home windows open for ventilation
Some members of the general public may experience health effects, and sensitive groups more serious ones
The value is an average of pollution levels over the past year rather than today's conditions

rationales.whyCorrect: The AQI is a 0 to 500 scale reported for criteria pollutants including PM2.5, and EPA officially describes the red 151 to 200 band as 'Unhealthy: some members of the general public may experience health effects; members of sensitive groups may experience more serious health effects.' A value of 165 therefore signals risk extending beyond people with known disease, while sensitive groups for particle pollution, including children, older adults, pregnant people, and those with asthma, COPD, or cardiovascular disease, face greater harm. The AQI reports current or same-day forecast conditions rather than an annual average, which is what makes it actionable. Recommended action at this level is to reduce prolonged or heavy outdoor exertion, keep windows and doors closed, and use filtration or recirculated air, so option B states the reverse of correct practice.
rationales.eli10: The AQI is a traffic light for air, and the color tells you who has to change plans. Orange means vulnerable people should ease off. Red means the air is dirty enough that ordinary healthy people feel it too, while vulnerable people are hit much harder. The second thing to hold onto is timing: this number describes right now, the way a rain forecast does, which is why it comes with instructions for today such as shortening the run and closing the windows.

questions.stem: A nursing student drives slowly through an assigned neighborhood and records housing condition, vacant lots, traffic patterns, sidewalk presence, parks, and the types of food stores available. Which community assessment method is being used?

options.text: Focus group discussion
Windshield survey
Community forum
Key informant interview

rationales.whyCorrect: A windshield survey is systematic direct observation of a community conducted from a moving vehicle, or on foot as a walking survey, to gather primary data about the physical and social environment: boundaries, housing quality, open space, transportation, commerce, services, signage, and visible signs of community life. It captures conditions residents may not think to mention and that census files, vital statistics, and other secondary data sets do not record, and it typically precedes and shapes the questions later put to residents. The other three are legitimate assessment methods but all collect data by asking people: a focus group elicits guided discussion among a small group of residents, a key informant interview draws on the perspective of a leader or service provider, and a community forum is an open public meeting.
rationales.eli10: A clinician sizes up a patient before asking a single question, noting color, breathing, and how they walk in. A windshield survey is that same first look applied to an entire neighborhood: go slowly, observe systematically, and write down what is actually there. It cannot tell you what living there feels like, so it does not replace talking with residents. It tells you what to ask them about.

questions.stem: A city's public water system must routinely test for contaminants, report results to customers, and notify residents when limits are exceeded. Under United States law, which agency sets the enforceable standards these public water systems must meet?

options.text: The Food and Drug Administration, under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act
The Environmental Protection Agency, under the federal Safe Drinking Water Act
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration, under the Occupational Safety and Health Act
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, under the Public Health Service Act

rationales.whyCorrect: The Safe Drinking Water Act authorizes EPA to issue National Primary Drinking Water Regulations, which set enforceable maximum contaminant levels or required treatment techniques and mandate monitoring, recordkeeping, public notification, and annual Consumer Confidence Reports for community water systems. Most states then apply for and receive primacy to enforce those standards and may adopt stricter ones. FDA regulates bottled water as a packaged food under the FD&C Act and generally aligns its limits with EPA's, OSHA regulates workplace exposures, and CDC conducts surveillance and outbreak investigation and issues guidance that is authoritative but not enforceable. Distinguishing binding regulation from advisory guidance is essential when evaluating any environmental health claim, and note that private wells fall outside the Act entirely, leaving testing to the owner unless state or local law requires it.
rationales.eli10: Different rulebooks cover different water. Water from your kitchen tap belongs to EPA under the Safe Drinking Water Act, with limits a utility can be penalized for exceeding. Water sealed in a bottle counts as food, so it belongs to FDA. CDC investigates outbreaks and publishes recommendations that carry expertise but no penalty. And a private well sits outside that federal rulebook, so unless the state or county has its own well rules, nobody is testing it unless the owner arranges it.

questions.stem: During the same heat wave, two neighborhoods in one city record similar daytime high temperatures, but one neighborhood has much warmer overnight temperatures and far more heat-related emergency visits. Which explanation best accounts for this difference?

options.text: Overnight temperature has little bearing on heat illness, because the body recovers fully during sleep
The neighborhood lies at a higher elevation, where thinner air holds daytime heat well past sunset
The neighborhood has more tree canopy and parkland, which traps warm humid air near the ground at night
Extensive pavement and dark roofs with little tree canopy store daytime heat and re-radiate it overnight

rationales.whyCorrect: Dark, impervious surfaces such as asphalt paving and roofing combine high solar absorption with high thermal mass: they take in radiation all day and release it slowly for hours after sunset, while sparse tree canopy removes both shade and the evaporative cooling that vegetation provides. The result is an urban heat island, which is typically most pronounced in nighttime minimum temperatures. Sustained warm nights are a principal driver of heat morbidity and mortality because the body loses the recovery period in which it normally offloads accumulated heat, and the risk is amplified where air conditioning is unavailable or unaffordable. Because canopy cover and impervious surface are distributed unevenly, differences of several degrees between blocks of one city are common. Option C reverses the actual effect of canopy, which lowers both surface and air temperature.
rationales.eli10: Touch a parking lot after dark, then the grass beside it. The asphalt is still handing back the day and the grass is not. Hard dark surfaces bank heat, while leaves shed it, partly by evaporating water the way sweating cools skin. A neighborhood that is mostly pavement and roof with little shade never finishes cooling, so the cool night a body needs to unload the day's heat never arrives. Heat injury accumulates, and the missing night is what tips people into the emergency department.

questions.stem: A health department finds elevated nitrate levels in private wells downstream from large livestock operations. It convenes agronomists, veterinarians, water engineers, ecologists, and public health nurses to trace the contamination across soil, animal, and human systems and to design one shared solution. What makes this a One Health approach rather than a conventional single-sector response?

options.text: It shifts responsibility for the contamination onto individual well owners, who must install filtration
It gives animal health outcomes priority over human outcomes, since livestock are the origin point
It treats human, animal, and environmental health as interconnected and has sectors act on one shared cause
It replaces clinical follow-up with environmental monitoring once the water source has been identified

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC defines One Health as a collaborative, multisectoral, and transdisciplinary approach working from local to global levels that recognizes the interconnection among people, animals, plants, and their shared environment. In this scenario one upstream agricultural practice, nitrogen applied as manure and fertilizer, moves through soil into groundwater and reappears as a human exposure, so no single sector can define or solve it: agronomy governs application rates, animal science governs herd density and waste handling, hydrology governs transport, and nursing and medicine govern case finding and follow-up. The defining feature is joint problem definition with simultaneous action on a shared cause, not sequential handoffs, burden shifting to residents, or substituting environmental testing for clinical evaluation. The stakes are concrete: nitrate carries a maximum contaminant level of 10 mg/L as nitrogen under the Safe Drinking Water Act because of infant methemoglobinemia, yet private wells are exempt from that Act, so detection depends on the health department rather than a utility.
rationales.eli10: Nitrogen spread on a field does not stop at the fence line. One Health treats the people, the herd, and the watershed as one system, so every sector sits at the same table and the practice at the top of the chain changes instead of symptoms at the bottom being managed forever.
